title: Here's How Much $10,000 in Altria Stock Pays You Each Year
detail:
Here's How Much $10,000 in Altria Stock Pays You Each Year
Thomas Niel, The Motley Fool

MO
^GSPC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Altria Group (NYSE: MO), parent company of Marlboro maker Philip Morris USA, has one of the highest forward yields among stocks in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC). It has also raised its quarterly dividend annually for 57 consecutive years, placing it among the Dividend Kings, stocks with at least 50 years of consecutive dividend growth.

While this company's days of high growth are behind it, a path remains for the stock to sustain and keep on slightly growing its quarterly payouts in the years ahead. Dividend investors should still consider it a buy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What a $10,000 investment in Altria can generate in annual dividend income

With Altria trading for around $78 per share, a $10,000 investment in the stock equates to around a 128-share position. Altria pays a $1.11-per-share quarterly dividend. Annualized, that comes out to $4.44 per share. Multiply that by 128 shares, and you get $568.32 in annual dividend income, giving it a 5.7% annual dividend yield. That's over 5 times the annual dividend yield of the S&P 500, which currently stands at around 1.1%.

Altria most recently declared a dividend increase in August, raising the quarterly payout by 4.7%. This is in line with management's current dividend growth policy, which targets "mid-single-digit dividend per share growth annually."

Why Altria stands to sustain its dividend stalwart status

Yes, Altria's 88.5% payout ratio looks very high. However, with rising cigarette prices and growing sales of "smokeless" products, the company's dividend policy appears sustainable.

Altria recently raised its full-year earnings growth guidance to between 4.5% and 6%, bolstering confidence that the company can both maintain its dividend and keep raising it at a modest pace in the years ahead.

"Going smokeless" remains a greater challenge for Altria than the success competitors like Philip Morris International have had in this area, but as sales of its smokeless products continue to help augment overall growth, the stock appears well positioned to maintain its status as both a high-yield dividend stock and a Dividend King.

title: Why Centrus Energy Stock Crashed 26% in October

Why Centrus Energy Stock Crashed 26% in October
Scott Levine, The Motley Fool

^GSPC
NVDA

Limping toward the end of 2026, Centrus Energy (NYSE:LEU) stock fell 18.6% in September and continued to decline last month. Analysts took a more bearish stance on the nuclear stock, and investors were clearly paying attention.

According to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence, Centrus Energy stock fell 26% in October, while the S&P 500 dipped 0.5%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Firms are skeptical of the company's acquisition of a key supplier

On Oct. 19, Centrus announced its acquisition of Westerman Holdings, which the company characterizes as one of its largest and most diversified suppliers. Centrus believes that the transaction, funded with about $95 million in cash and $21 million in equity, will contribute to its adjusted earnings per share in the first year following its closing.

Centrus lauded the acquisition as "a significant milestone ... as it builds supply chain resilience while diversifying its revenue base." Westerman provides Centrus to a variety of industries beyond nuclear, including oil and gas and other industrial sectors.

Investors immediately expressed their disapproval of the acquisition. Centrus shares dropped more than 4% on Oct. 19 from the stock's previous close.

On Oct. 20, analysts began to weigh in on the acquisition -- and the opinions were hardly encouraging. Roth Capital slashed its price target on Centrus to $115 from $188, maintaining a neutral rating. According to Thefly.com, the firm updated its model after Centrus acquired Westerman Holdings and believes that the company's third-quarter financial results could disappoint investors.

In the ensuing days, firms shared a variety of other downwardly revised price targets.

On Oct. 20, Barclays lowered its price target to $150 from $207.

On Oct. 23, UBS dropped its price target to $120 from $185.

On Oct. 26, JPMorgan reduced its price target to $120 from $180.

Centrus is a leading provider of nuclear fuel and services for the nuclear power industry. One area in which the company distinguishes itself is the production of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), a specialized form of nuclear fuel required by small modular reactors (SMRs), the next generation of nuclear reactors. At the end of September 2026, Centrus reported a backlog of $5.4 billion for both low-enriched uranium (LEU) and HALEU businesses.

title: No Matter What Happens to the S&P 500 in November, These 3 Dividend Stocks Belong in Your Portfolio
detail:
No Matter What Happens to the S&P 500 in November, These 3 Dividend Stocks Belong in Your Portfolio
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 11:01 AM CST 6 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

November has a way of making investors feel like they need an opinion about the market. The index is near a record, the AI trade is wobbling, and every headline wants you to decide whether this is the top. Nobody knows, and the portfolios that can thrive during the long stretches of uncertainty share one trait: They include a healthy helping of reliable dividend payers.

The three consumer companies below have paid and raised their dividends through recessions, pandemics, and the bursting of more than one market bubble. Two of them are in the middle of the biggest deals in their histories. All three sell things people keep restocking for their homes in good months and bad.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Target: 55 straight years of dividend raises and a store that still matters

In June, discount retail giant Target (NYSE: TGT) increased its quarterly dividend by 1.8% to $1.16 per share, making 2026 the 55th straight year it has raised its payout. At the current share price of near $163, that works out to a yield just over 3%, but the dividend still consumes less than half of its earnings, which leaves the company plenty of room to conduct share buybacks and invest in the stores themselves.

The reason Target belongs in retail investors' portfolios is not the yield alone. It is that the company keeps acting like a retailer that expects to be around for another 55 years. This fall, it relaunched Threshold, its house brand for home goods, finished a full remodel of its SoHo store in Manhattan, and promoted a shopping list showing that folks could pull together a Thanksgiving dinner for six in its stores for just $30.

The chain's dividend-hiking streak started in 1971, which means Target raised its payouts through every market the S&P 500 has produced since Richard Nixon was president.

2. McCormick: A 4% yield from the spice rack

Spice and sauce powerhouse McCormick (NYSE: MKC) is paying a quarterly dividend of $0.48 per share, up from $0.45 per share a year ago, and has raised its dividend annually for 40 consecutive years. From its 2020 peak above $100, the stock has fallen to about $48 today, which pushed its yield up to nearly 4%, the highest it has been in a generation.

What has investors nervous this year -- and what contributed to its year-to-date decline of around 28% in the stock -- is McCormick's pending combination with Unilever's foods business, which the two companies announced in March. That deal would create a company with about $20 billion in annual revenue, with roughly $600 million in expected cost savings, according to Reuters. It's slated to close by mid-2027.

Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, with AI chip designers and memory makers among the hardest hit. The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped 3% for its best session of 2026 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. By mid-session Thursday, the index was heading for its worst second day after a midterm election in data going back to 1896, the outlet noted.

Boeing (BA): A Top 10 Dow Stock for 2027 With a Record $745B of Orders
The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week, the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares, which left the Dow looking like the market's relative winner. On Thursday, that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular. You might also be interested in reading our piece on how the AI chip leader's growth compares with the cloud software giant's.

The reversal was fast and violent. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes on Thursday to erase its entire post-election rally, and even Wednesday's winners such as the iPhone maker turned lower. That Wednesday buying had been helped by falling oil prices, while the Windows maker jumped 6% to a record high.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the US added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. For a closer look at one of the biggest AI spenders caught in the sell-off, we recently covered why the search giant's low price-to-earnings ratio can mislead. The stronger jobs data lifted Treasury yields and kept Federal Reserve policy at the center of market attention, Reuters reported on November 6, as the price-weighted index of 30 major US companies held roughly flat.
